debriefing.title: Thank you!
debriefing.text: This study is a follow-up study for a series of our previous studies. In our previous studies, we wanted to know if “causes to break” and “break” mean the same thing. Though many researchers think they do, children may think they don’t. We found that when hearing a story where Suzy was riding her bike, hit Andy and he fell into the fence and it broke, young children, e.g. 4 and 5 year olds, say that Suzy caused the fence to break and Andy broke it. Similarly, when told that Sophia scared Bobby and he fell into a mirror and the mirror cracked, children said that Sophia caused the mirror to crack and that Bobby cracked it. These findings suggest that young children don’t think that “causes to break” and “break” mean the same thing. Note that “causing to break” and “break” are both statements about causation. So in saying that, for instance, Suzy caused the fence to break and that Andy broke it, we are making two different causal judgments. And if we are making two different causal judgments this raises questions about how we resolve responsibility. Most researchers think that being responsible for an outcome requires that you caused the outcome to occur. But how do we decide responsibility when making two different causal judgments? Though nobody has examined this question, we think our findings will make a contribution to understanding how, over development, we resolve issues of responsibility when making different causal judgments. Although children’s answers can vary, there aren’t any “right” or “wrong” answers to the questions. We are just interested in looking at the average responses from children and we won’t take any specific answers as “good” or “bad”. If you are interested in learning more about this, please see the following experimental paper with adults here. Thank you again for your participation!

blocks.title: 1. Overview of what we're doing today

listblocks.text: All together, it will take about 8-10 minutes to finish this study.
I’m going to ask your child some questions and I just want to know what they think.
There aren’t any right or wrong answers, so please let your child answer in the way that makes sense to them.

blocks.title: 2. Adjust your speakers
blocks.text: Please try playing this sample audio to make sure you'll be able to hear the story.

mediaBlock.warningText: Please try playing the sample audio.

webcamBlocks.title: 3. Make sure we can see you

listblocks.text: Take a look at your webcam view above. Get comfy, and adjust your own position or the computer as needed so both you and your child are visible.
This isn't a Skype call - no one in the lab can see you - but the recorded video of your participation will be sent to the lab to help with data analysis.

video-consent.risk_statement: There are no expected risks to participation.
video-consent.datause: A research assistant will watch your video and mark down your child's answers as well as other information such as interactions between you and your child during the story.
video-consent.payment: After you finish the study, we will email you a $5 Amazon gift card within approximately 3-5 business days. Please note that the gift card is for US residents only, but we still invite non-US residents to participate.
video-consent.purpose: This study is about how children use causal verbs in language and how they think about causation and responsibility.
video-consent.procedures: In this study your child will view a digital story and answer several questions by clicking on pictures on the screen. We will ask you to avoid discussing the answers with your child until the end of the study.
video-consent.institution: The Markman Lab of Stanford University
